title: Harlow Fresh Markets — reversing the margin decline
decision_question: How should Harlow reverse its declining operating margin, and which actions should it take first?

initial_hypothesis.statement: Wage inflation is the main cause; cut store labor hours 8% and freeze e-commerce.
initial_hypothesis.explanation: Store labor explains only about $4.5M of the $32.6M decline in operating income (FY2023→FY2025). The largest drivers are e-commerce fulfillment ($12.6M), promotions ($10.5M) and shrink ($7.5M). Wage rates rose but hours per $1,000 of sales fell, and low-labor stores show the highest shrink, so an 8% hours cut risks raising shrink. Freezing e-commerce leaves a loss-making service as it is. A good answer revises the diagnosis.

key_insights.text: Bridge FY2023→FY2025 (at FY2025 sales): sales growth +$2.8M; e-commerce fulfillment $-12.6M; promotions $-10.5M; shrink $-7.5M; store labor $-4.5M; occupancy/energy $-3.0M; private label +$2.7M. Labor is about 14% of the decline.

E-commerce loses money: net fulfillment cost $18.1M in FY2025 ($13.61 per order) against only about $7.7M of contribution on the 30% of e-commerce sales that are incremental: a net drag of about $10.4M a year.

The fee test shows a lever: higher fee and threshold cut delivered orders 9% but raised fee per delivered order from $3.10 to $6.40 and shifted orders to click-and-collect, at a 2% loss of e-commerce sales (mostly cannibalised anyway).

Labor cuts conflict with shrink: lowest-labor quartile has shrink of 3.1% vs 2.3% in the highest; an 8% hours cut (~$14.5M) could be partly offset by higher shrink (each 0.1 pp of shrink is about $1.5M).
Promotional growth is partly a competitive response to ValuMart (−4.2% comps near new stores), and vendor funding fell; 38% of events lose money — cut the losing events rather than all promotions.

Closing the nine weakest stores at lease expiry improves operating income by about $6.6M a year when all nine are closed (removing −$3.1M EBITDA plus 25% × $118M × 12% transferred), but three need a $7.5M exit cost and a board vote.
Target: 3.0% of ~$1.5B sales needs roughly $45M operating income, about $30M more than FY2025; the plan must add up to that within $25M one-time cost and protect the $20M FY2026 covenant.

The e-commerce team's 6.1% (≈$7.8M) leaves out third-party delivery (≈$8.3M net of fees) and cannibalisation; with delivery alone it is ≈$-0.5M, and counting only incremental sales the service is a ≈$10M drag.

required_calculations.expected: sales_growth_at_2023_margin: +2.8; shrink: -7.5; promotions: -10.5; private_label: +2.7; store_labor: -4.5; occupancy_energy: -3.0; ecommerce_fulfillment: -12.6; total: -32.6
required_calculations.tolerance: each driver ±$1M; ranking must be right (e-com, promo, shrink > labor)

required_calculations.text: E-commerce net cost per order and economics

required_calculations.expected: ≈ $29.8M more operating income at FY2025 sales

decision_relevant_evidence.text: Income statement lines showing which costs grew as a share of sales
E-commerce per-order costs, fees and 70% cannibalisation
Promotional share, 14 pp margin gap, vendor funding fall, 38% losing events
ValuMart competitive pressure and price perception

contradictory_evidence: Hourly wages rose 9.4%, yet labor as a share of sales rose only 0.3 pp because hours per $1,000 fell
Promotions hurt margin but defend traffic against ValuMart
Owners want to keep delivery, but it loses money
E-commerce team's 6.1% margin vs the fulfillment line and cannibalisation

reasoning_traps.text: Accepting 'wage inflation is the main cause' because the hourly wage rose 9%
Treating e-commerce sales growth as success without counting cannibalisation and fulfillment cost
Recommending deep labor cuts without considering shrink and service effects
Cutting all promotions without considering the competitive response
A list of levers without sizing that does not add up to the 3.0% target
Accepting the e-commerce team's '6.1% contribution margin' claim
Reading 'stores with deeper promotions grew faster' as proof that promotions pay (no control for store mix; the post-event review says 38% of events lose money)

key_tradeoffs.text: Labor savings vs shrink and service
Promotional margin vs traffic defence against ValuMart
Keeping delivery (owners) vs its economics — reprice/redesign rather than freeze or kill
Store closures (savings) vs lease-exit cost and the board-vote commitment

plausible_recommendations.text: Sized plan led by e-commerce redesign (fees/threshold, shift to click-and-collect, renegotiate delivery), shrink reduction, promotional pruning of losing events and private-label growth, with weak-store closures at lease expiry; labor productivity only where it does not raise shrink.
Plan that includes some labor-hour reduction — defensible if targeted (e.g. scheduling, self-checkout) and the shrink risk is acknowledged and sized.
Exit home delivery and keep click-and-collect — defensible with the economics, if the owners' commitment is addressed.
The management plan as written (8% hours cut + e-commerce freeze) as the main answer.

defensibility_criteria: Diagnosis rests on a quantified bridge, not on the most visible cost
Actions are sized and add up (roughly) to the 3.0% target, with the covenant in view
Second-order effects (shrink from labor cuts, traffic from promo cuts) are acknowledged
